Binary Search.problem: Find any occurrence of x in a nondecreasing array, returning index or -1.
Binary Search.approach: Comparison with the middle discards a half that cannot contain x. The interval length strictly decreases.
Binary Search.pitfalls: Use l+(r-l)/2 to avoid addition overflow. A duplicate result need not be first.

Lower Bound.problem: On a nondecreasing array return first index with value >= x, or length if absent.
Lower Bound.approach: Use half-open [l,r). The answer is never excluded: qualifying mid keeps the left half including mid; a nonqualifying mid moves l past mid. l==r is the insertion boundary.
Lower Bound.trace: For [1,2,2,4], lower boundary for 2 is 1 and upper is 3.
Lower Bound.pitfalls: Empty array returns 0. Boundary index length is valid as a result but cannot be dereferenced.
Lower Bound.alternatives: A scan is O(n); binary search exploits sorted order.

Upper Bound.problem: On a nondecreasing array return first index with value > x, or length if absent.
Upper Bound.approach: Use half-open [l,r). The answer is never excluded: qualifying mid keeps the left half including mid; a nonqualifying mid moves l past mid. l==r is the insertion boundary.
Upper Bound.trace: For [1,2,2,4], lower boundary for 2 is 1 and upper is 3.
Upper Bound.pitfalls: Empty array returns 0. Boundary index length is valid as a result but cannot be dereferenced.
Upper Bound.alternatives: A scan is O(n); binary search exploits sorted order.

Search Insert Position.problem: On a nondecreasing array return first index with value >= x, or length if absent.
Search Insert Position.approach: Use half-open [l,r). The answer is never excluded: qualifying mid keeps the left half including mid; a nonqualifying mid moves l past mid. l==r is the insertion boundary.
Search Insert Position.trace: For [1,2,2,4], lower boundary for 2 is 1 and upper is 3.
Search Insert Position.pitfalls: Empty array returns 0. Boundary index length is valid as a result but cannot be dereferenced.
Search Insert Position.alternatives: A scan is O(n); binary search exploits sorted order.

Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array.problem: Return [floor value <=x, ceil value >=x] as OptionalInts; either may be absent.
Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array.approach: Floor is the value just before upper bound; ceil is the value at lower bound.
Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array.trace: For x=4 lower=2, upper=2; a[1]=3 and a[2]=5.
Floor and Ceil in Sorted Array.pitfalls: Floor/ceil are values, not indices. OptionalInt avoids collision with a valid -1.

First and Last Occurrence.problem: Return first/last indices of x, or [-1,-1].
First and Last Occurrence.approach: Equal values occupy [lowerBound,upperBound), so the inclusive last is upper-1.
First and Last Occurrence.trace: The block of 2 is indices [1,4), giving [1,3].
First and Last Occurrence.pitfalls: When lower==upper the value is absent, including empty input.

Count Occurrences in Sorted Array.problem: Count occurrences of x in a nondecreasing array.
Count Occurrences in Sorted Array.approach: Subtract lower from upper boundary of the equal-value block.
Count Occurrences in Sorted Array.pitfalls: Absent values give equal bounds and count zero.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array I.problem: Search a rotated nondecreasing array of distinct values; return index or -1.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array I.approach: At least one side of mid is sorted. Check whether target lies in that sorted interval; keep that side or the other. Equal endpoints/mid can hide the sorted side, so trim endpoints for the duplicate variant.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array I.trace: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]: left of 7 is sorted, but 0 lies outside; search right and find index 4.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array I.pitfalls: Distinct-input reasoning alone cannot resolve all-equal endpoints. Shrinking duplicates degrades worst-case time to linear.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.problem: Search a rotated nondecreasing array allowing duplicates; return existence.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.approach: At least one side of mid is sorted. Check whether target lies in that sorted interval; keep that side or the other. Equal endpoints/mid can hide the sorted side, so trim endpoints for the duplicate variant.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.complexity: O(n) worst time with duplicates; O(1) space.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.trace: [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]: left of 7 is sorted, but 0 lies outside; search right and find index 4.
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II.pitfalls: Distinct-input reasoning alone cannot resolve all-equal endpoints. Shrinking duplicates degrades worst-case time to linear.

Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.problem: For a nonempty rotated array of DISTINCT values return its minimum value.
Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.approach: Compare mid with right: if mid is greater, the rotation break is to its right; otherwise mid may be the minimum, so retain it.
Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.trace: mid at value 1 <= right 3, keep left including mid; answer index 2.
Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array.pitfalls: With duplicates use r-- when a[mid]==a[r], with O(n) worst time. Distinctness is required by this implementation.

Rotation Count.problem: For a nonempty rotated array of DISTINCT values return number of right rotations modulo n (the minimum index).
Rotation Count.approach: Compare mid with right: if mid is greater, the rotation break is to its right; otherwise mid may be the minimum, so retain it.
Rotation Count.trace: mid at value 1 <= right 3, keep left including mid; answer index 2.
Rotation Count.pitfalls: With duplicates use r-- when a[mid]==a[r], with O(n) worst time. Distinctness is required by this implementation.

Single Element in Sorted Array.problem: A sorted odd-length array has one single value; every other value appears exactly twice. Return the single.
Single Element in Sorted Array.approach: Before the single, pairs start at even indices. Force mid to be even: if mid/mid+1 match, the single is later; otherwise it is at or before mid.
Single Element in Sorted Array.trace: For [1,1,2,3,3,4,4], even mid 2 mismatches 3; left half contains single 2.
Single Element in Sorted Array.pitfalls: Contract requires exactly paired other values. Singleton input is valid.

Square Root of a Number.approach: Search the largest m with m²<=n. Check m<=n/m to avoid multiplication overflow.
Square Root of a Number.pitfalls: Search starts at 1, so division by zero is impossible; n=0 leaves answer 0.

Nth Root of a Number.problem: Return the exact nonnegative integer nth root for power>=1 and value>=0, or -1.
Nth Root of a Number.approach: Binary search the base. During exponentiation, stop before a multiply would exceed value; this both caps work and avoids overflow.
Nth Root of a Number.trace: 3³=27, so base 3 is an exact match.
Nth Root of a Number.pitfalls: Do not use floating-point equality for exact roots. Zero root is handled separately.

Koko Eating Bananas.problem: Each nonempty pile consumes ceil(pile/speed) whole hours. Find smallest integer speed within hours, or -1 when impossible.
Koko Eating Bananas.approach: Feasibility is monotone: faster never needs more time. Binary search the first feasible speed between 1 and largest pile.
Koko Eating Bananas.complexity: O(n log maxPile) time; O(1) space.
Koko Eating Bananas.pitfalls: Use long for ceiling arithmetic and totals. One hour per nonempty pile is a necessary lower bound.

Minimum Days to Make Bouquets.problem: Make m bouquets using k adjacent, disjoint bloomed flowers each; find earliest day or -1. Bloom days are nonnegative.
Minimum Days to Make Bouquets.approach: For a day, count disjoint groups of k within bloomed runs. Later days can only add usable flowers, giving monotone feasibility.
Minimum Days to Make Bouquets.complexity: O(n log dayRange) time; O(1) space.
Minimum Days to Make Bouquets.trace: Day 3 blooms positions 0,2,4, enough for three single-flower bouquets.
Minimum Days to Make Bouquets.pitfalls: m*k needs long. Breaking adjacency resets the run; do not count merely the total bloomed flowers.

Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold.problem: For nonnegative values, find the smallest positive divisor d for which sum ceil(a[i]/d)<=threshold.
Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold.approach: The ceiling sum is nonincreasing as divisor increases. Search its first threshold-satisfying point.
Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold.complexity: O(n log maxValue) time; O(1) space.
Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold.pitfalls: An all-zero array admits divisor 1. Threshold smaller than the count of positive values is impossible.

Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days.problem: Partition nonnegative ordered weights/pages/lengths into at most parts contiguous groups; minimize the largest group sum. Return long.
Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days.approach: Given a candidate maximum, greedily fill each group until the next item would exceed it. This uses the fewest groups for that maximum. Feasibility becomes true monotonically as the maximum increases.
Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days.trace: At capacity 18, groups [7,2,5] sum 14 and [10,8] sum 18. Capacity 17 needs three groups.
Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days.pitfalls: No reordering or splitting individual items. Books rejects more students than books. Painter time multipliers belong outside this common partition kernel. Negative values violate greedy monotonicity.
Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days.alternatives: Enumerating every cut placement is exponential. DP over position and number of groups is O(parts*n²).

Kth Missing Positive Number.problem: Given strictly increasing positive integers, return kth missing positive, k>=1.
Kth Missing Positive Number.approach: Missing count before a[i] is a[i]-(i+1). Binary search the first count at least k. Before that boundary, l actual values shift the answer to k+l.
Kth Missing Positive Number.trace: Missing positives are 1,5,6,8,9; the fifth is 9.
Kth Missing Positive Number.pitfalls: Input must be positive, sorted and distinct; empty input returns k. Overflow is explicitly rejected.

Aggressive Cows.problem: Choose cows stall positions maximizing their minimum pairwise distance. Require 2<=cows<=stall count.
Aggressive Cows.approach: Sort stalls. For a candidate distance place each next cow at the earliest possible stall; choosing earlier cannot reduce future options. Search the last feasible distance.
Aggressive Cows.complexity: O(n log n+n log coordinateRange) time; O(n) copy space.
Aggressive Cows.trace: Sorted 1,2,4,8,9: distance 3 permits 1,4,8; distance 4 permits only 1,8.
Aggressive Cows.pitfalls: Use long coordinate differences for negative and extreme int coordinates. One cow has no pairwise minimum, so it is rejected.

Find Peak Element.problem: Return a STRICT local maximum index, assuming adjacent values are unequal and outside boundaries are -infinity.
Find Peak Element.approach: An ascending slope guarantees some peak to the right; a descending slope guarantees one on the left including mid. Retain that side.
Find Peak Element.trace: [1,2,3,1]: slope 2<3 goes right; slope 3>1 keeps index 2.
Find Peak Element.pitfalls: Without the unequal-neighbor assumption, this finds a weak peak and may not satisfy a strict-peak judge.

Allocate Books.problem: Partition nonnegative ordered weights/pages/lengths into exactly parts nonempty contiguous groups; minimize the largest group sum. Return long.
Allocate Books.approach: Given a candidate maximum, greedily fill each group until the next item would exceed it. This uses the fewest groups for that maximum. Feasibility becomes true monotonically as the maximum increases.
Allocate Books.trace: At capacity 18, groups [7,2,5] sum 14 and [10,8] sum 18. Capacity 17 needs three groups.
Allocate Books.pitfalls: No reordering or splitting individual items. Books rejects more students than books. Painter time multipliers belong outside this common partition kernel. Negative values violate greedy monotonicity.
Allocate Books.alternatives: Enumerating every cut placement is exponential. DP over position and number of groups is O(parts*n²).

Minimize Maximum Distance Between Gas St.problem: Add at most k stations at arbitrary real positions to minimize the largest consecutive gap.
Minimize Maximum Distance Between Gas St.approach: For gap g and candidate d, ceil(g/d)-1 new stations suffice. Sum required stations and binary search the first feasible real distance using 80 iterations.
Minimize Maximum Distance Between Gas St.complexity: O(n log n+80*n) time; O(n) copy space.
Minimize Maximum Distance Between Gas St.trace: Gap 10 with one station splits at 5, yielding maximum gap 5.
Minimize Maximum Distance Between Gas St.pitfalls: Floating-point comparisons are approximate; the returned value is intended for a judge tolerance such as 1e-6. Exact multiples require ceil-1, not floor.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays.problem: Return the median of the sorted multiset union; at least one array must be nonempty.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.approach: Use logarithmic kth-selection. Odd length takes the middle rank; even length averages both middle ranks.
Median of Two Sorted Arrays.pitfalls: Widen before adding middle int values. Both empty arrays have no median.

Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.problem: Return the ONE-based kth smallest entry of the combined sorted arrays, counting duplicates.
Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.approach: Partition both arrays with exactly k entries on the left. A valid partition has left maxima <= opposite right minima; its largest left value is the kth entry.
Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.trace: For k=5, left sides [2,3,6] and [1,4] contain five values; max left is 6.
Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.pitfalls: Use long infinities so real MIN_VALUE/MAX_VALUE are not confused with boundaries. Both arrays must be sorted.
Kth Element of Two Sorted Arrays.alternatives: A two-pointer merge can stop at k in O(k) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Row with Maximum Ones.problem: Each binary row is nondecreasing; return the first row with the most ones, or -1 if no ones.
Row with Maximum Ones.approach: First one is lowerBound(1); subtract from row length and retain a strict improvement so ties choose the first row.
Row with Maximum Ones.trace: Row counts are 1,2,0, so row 1 wins.
Row with Maximum Ones.pitfalls: Rows need to be sorted. An all-zero matrix returns -1.
Row with Maximum Ones.alternatives: A staircase walk from the top-right can achieve O(rows+cols) for a rectangular row-sorted binary matrix.

Search a 2D Matrix I.problem: Rectangular matrix is globally sorted in row-major order: each row sorted and every new row starts after the previous row ends.
Search a 2D Matrix I.approach: Treat the matrix as a virtual sorted array; index m maps to row m/cols and column m%cols.
Search a 2D Matrix I.trace: Virtual array [1,3,5,7,9,11]; 9 is at flat index 4 -> (1,1).
Search a 2D Matrix I.pitfalls: Row/column sorting alone is insufficient; that requires Matrix II.

Search a 2D Matrix II.problem: Rectangular matrix has each row and column nondecreasing; search target.
Search a 2D Matrix II.approach: Start top-right. If current is too large, its column below is too large as well; discard the column. If too small, its row to the left is too small; discard the row.
Search a 2D Matrix II.trace: 7>6 move left to 4; 4<6 move down to 5; 5<6 move down to 6.
Search a 2D Matrix II.pitfalls: This staircase walk needs both row and column monotonicity.

Find Peak Element in a 2D Matrix.problem: Find a cell strictly larger than its four orthogonal neighbors; assume orthogonally adjacent values differ. Outside is -infinity.
Find Peak Element in a 2D Matrix.approach: Choose the maximum in the middle column, already larger than vertical neighbors. If a horizontal neighbor is larger, a peak exists toward that side; binary search columns.
Find Peak Element in a 2D Matrix.trace: Column 0 maximum is 3 at row 1; its right neighbor is 2 and vertical neighbor is 1, so (1,0) is a peak.
Find Peak Element in a 2D Matrix.pitfalls: Equal adjacent values violate the strict-peak assumption. Negative values are safe with long boundary sentinels.

Median of a Row Wise Sorted Matrix.problem: Return the median value of a rectangular row-sorted matrix with an odd number of cells.
Median of a Row Wise Sorted Matrix.approach: Search VALUE space. Count values <=mid using upper bounds in each row. The median is the smallest value with more than half the cells at or below it.
Median of a Row Wise Sorted Matrix.trace: Flattened sorted values 1,2,3,3,5,6,6,9,9; fifth value is 5.
Median of a Row Wise Sorted Matrix.pitfalls: Use long value bounds for the full signed-int range. This contract excludes even cell counts.
Median of a Row Wise Sorted Matrix.alternatives: Flatten and sort uses O(N log N) time and O(N) storage.
